Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 94, verses 1–4 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ ﴿And We removed from you your burden﴾ ﴿Which had weighed down your back﴾ ﴿And We raised high for you your remembrance﴾.

This is a rhetorical question (istifham taqriri, a question that seeks affirmation of what it asserts) built on a negation. Its purpose is to establish the affirmative of what is negated, as was mentioned more than once before. This affirmation is meant as a reminder, so that the Prophet (ﷺ) would keep this favour in mind when a tightness of breast overcomes him because of the harm he suffers from a people whom he wishes well, whom he wants to save from the Fire and whose standing among the nations he wants to raise. Thus he would persist in his great call energetic, without grief or distress.

The literal meaning of sharh (expanding) is separating the parts of flesh from one another. From it come shurayha (a slice of meat) and tashrih (dissection in medicine). It is also applied to the soul's acceptance of, and contentment with, the state it is in. The apparent sense of the words in al-Asas (Asas al-Balagha) is that this is a literal usage. Perhaps he took into account its frequent use, that is, it is among the metaphors that have become equal to the literal meaning. For the apparent sense is that literal sharh is specific to cutting flesh, and that applying sharh to the soul's contentment with a state originates as a metaphor (isti'ara), arising from the use of the word "tightness" (ḍīq) and its derivatives for the feeling of sorrow and distress. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And your breast is constrained by it lest they say, "Why has not a treasure been sent down to him?"﴾ [Hud: 12], and so on. Thus the removal of sorrow from the soul is likened to the cutting of flesh. This is the more fitting reading in light of His words: ﴿Indeed, with hardship comes ease﴾ [al-Sharh: 5].

He had already mentioned His words: ﴿He said, "My Lord, expand for me my breast"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 25] in surah Ta-Ha.

So "breast" here refers to the inner perception that comprises the notions of intellect and understanding. Expanding his breast is a kinaya (metonymy) for bestowing upon him all the perfections to which his pure soul aspires, informing him of Allah's approval of him, and giving him good news of the victory that will come to the religion he brought.

This is the interpretation of the verse in accordance with what its composition implies and with its independence from external narrations. Ibn 'Abbas interpreted it as meaning that Allah expanded his heart with Islam. Al-Hasan said: "The expansion of his breast was that it was filled with knowledge and wisdom." Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah al-Tustari said: "He expanded his breast with the light of prophethood."

[Page 409]

Many of the mufassirun (commentators) took it in this sense, and Ibn 'Atiyya attributed it to the majority.

It is also possible to take sharh as a physical expansion. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he interpreted it this way, and this is the apparent practice of al-Tirmidhi, since he transmitted the hadith of the splitting of the Prophet's breast in his commentary on this surah. Thus the verse would be an allusion to reports about the splitting of the breast of the Prophet (ﷺ), a sacred splitting. Part of this report is transmitted in the two Sahihs, and it is transmitted at length in the Sira and the Masanid. Some narrations in the two Sahihs say that it occurred in a dream, and dreams of prophets are revelation. Other narrations say that it occurred while he was awake, and this is the apparent sense of what is in al-Bukhari. In Sahih Muslim, it is said that it occurred while he was awake and in the sight of boys his own age. In a hadith of Muslim from Anas ibn Malik, he said: "I saw the trace of the cut on the skin of the chest of the Prophet (ﷺ)." Some narrations say that the Prophet (ﷺ) was between sleeping and waking. The narrations differ concerning its time and place, although they agree that it took place in Makkah. The differences in the narrations led some scholars to hold that the splitting of his blessed breast was repeated two to four times, among them when he was with Halima. In the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal, the splitting occurred when the Prophet (ﷺ) was ten years old.

What is in the Sahih from Abu Dhar is that it occurred at the Mi'raj, when he was taken up to the heaven. Perhaps some of these events were a dream and some were physical. None of these reports, with their differing levels of authenticity, indicates that this is the expansion intended in the verse. Since that splitting was a miracle beyond the normal course, it may be what is intended, and this is what Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi preferred in al-Ahkam. In that case the word "breast" is used in its literal sense, namely the inner cavity that contains the heart. Some scholars interpreted "breast" as "heart," as 'Iyad related in al-Shifa, pointing to what came in the report of the splitting of the breast about removing his heart and taking out the seat of whispering from it. Both meanings of sharh indicate that it is the placing of a great meaning into the soul of the Prophet (ﷺ), either directly or by way of its implications, as is clear.

The lam in His words "for you" (laka) is the lam of causation, and it indicates the honouring of the Prophet (ﷺ), that Allah did this for his sake.

Mentioning the prepositional phrase before the object of expansion uses the method of ambiguity (ibham) to create suspense (tashwiq). When the verb "We expand" (nashrah) is mentioned, the listener knows that there is something to be expanded. When the phrase "for you" (laka) comes, the ambiguity grows stronger and the suspense increases, because "for you" conveys the sense of "something for your sake." When the phrase "your breast" (ṣadrak) follows it, the expected object is determined and settles firmly in the mind. This is what al-Kashshaf pointed to, and the author of al-Miftah followed it in the section on itnab (elaboration).

Al-wizr means hardship. Its "placing down" (wad') means removing it from the one who carries it. The expression is a tamthil (extended metaphor) for the removal of hardships and distresses by likening it to someone who sets down a load from his bearer in order to relieve him of the toil of the weight.

The meaning is that Allah removed from him everything that caused him distress from the customs of the people of ignorance (jahiliyya), which do not suit the purity and nobility with which Allah had created his soul, and from which he could not avoid conforming to them. So He set that down from him when He revealed the message to him. Likewise, the weight of revelation that he felt at the beginning of his mission was eased for him by His words: ﴿We will make you recite, and you will not forget﴾ [al-A'la: 6], up to His words: ﴿and We will ease you toward ease﴾ [al-A'la: 8].

"Anqaḍa" means to make a thing have a naqīḍ (creaking sound). The naqīḍ is the sound of the creaking of a saddle or pack-saddle, the sound of the bones of the joints, and the cracking of the fingers. Its intransitive verb is of the pattern naṣara, and it becomes transitive with the hamza.

Attributing "anqaḍa" to the wizr is a majaz 'aqli (rational metaphor). Its transitivity to "the back" (ẓahr) follows from likening hardship to a load. The construction is therefore a tamthil for one who bears severe hardships with a load weighing heavily on a pack animal, so heavily that the bones of its back give out a cracking and creaking sound. It is a wonderful tamthil, since it is a compound comparison that admits of being divided into its parts.

Describing the wizr with this description completes the tamthil, showing that it is a great burden.

Know that in His words ﴿anqaḍa ẓahrak﴾ the letters ḍād and ẓā' come together, and they are close in articulation. Pronouncing them together may produce some heaviness on the tongue, but this does not contradict eloquence, since it does not reach the level of what is called tanafur al-kalimat (cacophony of words). Rather, the like of it is excused in the speech of eloquent speakers. The Arabs are eloquent in their speech. So when the structure of the speech requires the occurrence of two such close letters, the eloquent speaker does not mind the slight heaviness that arises when they come together. A similar case is His words: ﴿and glorify Him﴾ [wa sabbiḥ-hu], in the combination of ḥā' with hā', where idgham (assimilation) is not valid. The scholars of tajwid (recitation rules) have recommended clearly pronouncing the ḍād separately from the ẓā' when they meet, as in this verse and in His words: ﴿And the wrongdoer will bite on his hands﴾ [al-Furqan: 27]. There are parallels to this in the Qur'an.

This verse is well known. The imams in the mosques have always been careful to avoid substituting one of these two letters for the other, because of the disagreement among the jurists about the invalidity of the prayer of one who makes errors in recitation (lahhan) and of one who does not recite well at all, or, if he does it intentionally, if he prays alone. Some also hold that the prayer of those behind him is invalid if the one making errors is the imam.

Raising the remembrance (raf' al-dhikr) means making his mention among people with attributes of perfection. This is achieved through what was revealed of the Qur'an as praise of him and as an honour, and by inspiring people to speak of the virtues Allah had placed in him from the beginning of his upbringing.

The conjunction of "And We removed" (wa waḍa'na) and "We raised" (wa rafa'na) in the past tense to the verb "We expand" (nashraḥ) in the present tense is because the particle lam has turned the present tense into the past. So the two verbs in the past tense are conjoined to it, since they fall within the scope of the affirmation. Because the particle lam does not accompany them, they are given the meaning of the past that the particle lam conveys.

The verse alludes to circumstances in which the Prophet (ﷺ) was in distress, or in which it was fitting that he be in distress, and that Allah removed from him the distress he had, or prepared his soul so that he would not be troubled by it.

The Prophet (ﷺ) knew these circumstances, as his being addressed in a rhetorical question that presupposes knowledge of what is affirmed indicates. Perhaps the detail of them was in what came before in surah al-Duha. These circumstances may have been his aversion to what the people of ignorance were upon, namely rejecting the tawhid of Allah and the evil of their deeds.

He was in distress about being among them, unable to turn them away from what they were in. He did not expect a way by which he could guide them, or he had not yet reached knowledge of the true reality of the truth to which his people should adhere. He hoped only for the salvation of his own soul, wishing to find for himself a spark of light that would illuminate for him the path of truth. This was what led him to reflect, to seclude himself, and to turn to Allah, so he would retreat in the cave of Hira'. When Allah rescued him from that quagmire by honouring him with revelation, this was an expansion of what had constricted his breast at that time. The light became clear to him, and he was commanded to save his people, whom he might think to be seekers of truth and pure souls. When they met his guidance with aversion, and his gentle dealing with them with disdain, another tightness arose in his breast, to which His words allude: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not become believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 3]. The revelation that continued to descend upon him concerning this matter tied his heart with words such as His, may He be exalted: ﴿Not upon you is their guidance, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 272]. So whenever a revelation of this kind descended upon him, it gave him an expansion of his breast.

The protection of Abu Talib, and his holding back of Quraysh from harming him, was a relief for him, and the strongest supporter of his call was one whose presence expanded his breast. Whenever a person from among the people became a believer, some of the tightness lessened from his breast. The severity of Quraysh against the believers would constrict his breast, so whenever some believers were freed from the harm of Quraysh, such as the manumission of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq of Bilal and others, and with what Allah gave him as good news of the outcome of victory for him and for the believers, both explicitly and allusively, like His words in the surah before it: ﴿And your Lord is going to give you, and you will be satisfied﴾ [al-Duha: 5], that is among the expansion intended here. The summary of the matter is that the manifestations of this expansion are numerous, and that they are a secret between Allah, may He be exalted, and His Messenger (ﷺ) who is addressed in this verse.

As for the removal of the burden from him, it was achieved by two things: by his guidance to the truth, which removed his bewilderment through reflection on the state of his people. This is what His words allude to: ﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾ [al-Duha: 7]. And by Allah sparing him the burden of the hardships of his livelihood, which might have occupied him from the intimacy he found in contemplating the reform of his soul. This is what His words allude to: ﴿And He found you poor and made you self-sufficient﴾ [al-Duha: 8].

The raising of the remembrance is a majaz (metaphor) for inspiring people to mention him favourably. This is achieved by creating the causes of that good reputation so that people speak of it. The word "raising" (raf') is borrowed for a good mention, because raising means making a thing high, out of the reach of all hands and not trampled by feet. Allah had created His Messenger (ﷺ) with noble qualities whose kind is rare, and no one attained the extent that he attained in them, to the point that he was called "the Trustworthy" among his people. It has been said that His words: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger﴾ [al-Takwir: 19], ﴿[who is] of power, with esteem near the Owner of the Throne﴾ [al-Takwir: 20], ﴿obeyed and trustworthy﴾ [al-Takwir: 21] refer to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Among the greatness of raising his remembrance is that his name is joined with the name of Allah, may He be exalted, in the word of Islam, which is the shahada (testimony of faith).

This interpretation has been transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, in the version of Ibn Hibban and Abu Ya'la. al-Suyuti said: "Its isnad is hasan (good)." 'Iyad related it in al-Shifa without an isnad. What is said about the mention of "for you" (laka) with "We raised" (wa rafa'na) is the same as what is said about its counterpart with His words: ﴿Did We not expand for you﴾.

Why was "lak" (for you) not mentioned together with "Wa wada'na 'anka wizraka" (And We removed from you your burden)? It is because "'anka" (from you) already suffices, for in conveying vagueness followed by specification it is equivalent to "lak" (for you). And in conveying care for the Prophet (ﷺ), it equals the word "lak", because the verb wada'a (to lay down/remove), when transitive to wizr (burden), already indicates that the laying down is "from him". So the addition of "'anka" is an elaboration (itnab) which indicates that this is an act of care for him, like his saying "lak" which precedes it. Thus, by mentioning "'anka", there is achieved both the completion of the transitivity of the verb wada'na (We removed), together with fulfilling the right of vagueness followed by clarification.

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that God the Exalted says: "I created one hardship, and I created two eases, and a hardship will never overcome two eases." End of quotation.

Hardship (*ʿusr*) is the difficulty in attaining what is desired and in carrying out the intended work.

Ease (*yusr*) is its opposite, namely: the facility of attaining what is desired and the absence of exhaustion in it.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, with hardship there is ease﴾ is an emphasis (*muʾakkida*) of the sentence ﴿So indeed, with hardship there is ease﴾. The benefit of this emphasis is to establish the constancy and generality of this promise, because it is a strange (*ʿajib*) announcement.

Some exegetes made the ease in the first sentence the ease of this world, and the ease in the second sentence the ease of the Hereafter. The style of Arabic speech does not support this, because the second sentence is purely an emphasis.

Moreover, the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "A hardship will never overcome two eases" has its wording and meaning bound to this verse. It is stated in some of its narrations that he recited this verse at that time, and the exegetes concurred in deriving that meaning from it. Therefore it is necessary to address this. It has become widespread among scholars that this is derived from the definiteness of the word "hardship" and its repetition in definite form, and from the indefiniteness of the word "ease" and its repetition in indefinite form. They said: when an indefinite word is repeated in indefinite form, the second is other than the first; when a word is repeated in definite form, the second is the same as the first, as in God's saying ﴿As We sent to Pharaoh a messenger﴾ (Al-Muzzammil 73:15) ﴿but Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger﴾ (Al-Muzzammil 73:16).

Basing their argument on the rule of repeating an indefinite noun in definite form is an error, because that rule concerns repeating an indefinite noun in definite form, not repeating a definite noun in definite form. It is also specific to the definite article of reference (*lam al-ʿahd*) and not the definite article of genus (*lam al-jins*). Further, it concerns repeating a word in a second statement, whereas what is in the verse is not the repetition of a word in a second statement; rather it is a repetition of the first sentence. So this objection should not be considered. Abu ʿAli al-Husayn al-Jurjani had already refuted it in his book *al-Nazm*, as in *Maʿalim al-Tanzil*. The author of *al-Kashshaf* also refuted it, and Ibn Hisham in *Mughni al-Labib* declared that rule an error.

What appears correct in explaining the meaning of the Prophet's saying "A hardship will never overcome two eases" is that the sentence ﴿Indeed, with hardship there is ease﴾ is an emphasis of the sentence ﴿So indeed, with hardship there is ease﴾. It is established that the purpose of emphasizing a sentence in such a case is to emphasize the ruling contained in the statement. There is no doubt that the ruling derived from this sentence is the establishment that ease joins hardship when it occurs. So the emphasis serves to affirm the precedence of the effect of ease over the effect of hardship. That precedence is expressed by the dual form in the phrase "two eases" (يُسْرَيْنِ). The dual here is a symbolic metonymy (*kināya ramziyya*) for dominance and superiority. The dual may be used as a metonym for repetition intended to indicate multiplicity, as in God's saying ﴿Then return the gaze twice; the gaze will return to you humbled and weary﴾ (Al-Mulk 67:4), meaning: "return the gaze many times," because the gaze does not become weary from two returns. Similarly is the Arabs' saying: *labbayka* ("at your service"), *saʿdayka* ("at your service repeatedly"), and *dawalayka* ("again and again"). Repetition entails the strength of the thing repeated, so strength is a necessary consequence of the necessary consequence of the dual form. When several such consequences are involved, the metonymy is symbolic.

This meaning is not derived from the definite article in "hardship," nor from the indefiniteness of "ease" and its repetition in indefinite form.

(Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah 94, verse 7)

"So when you are free, then labour" (﴿فَإذا فَرَغْتَ فانْصَبْ﴾).

This is a consequence of what has been established of the reminder of [divine] kindness and care, and of the promise to ease what is difficult for him in his obedience, the greatest of which is the conveying of the Message, without weariness or impatience.

Al-faraagh (free time, emptiness) is the emptiness of the inside of a container or vessel, because its nature is that it is filled.

The verb (faragha) implies that its doer was full of something, and a person's being free is a metaphor for completing what he is supposed to be doing.

The object of (﴿faraght﴾) is not mentioned here, and the context of the speech requires that it refers to the tasks the Messenger ﷺ undertakes, just as the thrust of the surah concerns the easing of the difficulties of the call and what surrounds it. The meaning is: when you have completed one of the major tasks, turn to another task so that it fills his time entirely with great undertakings. From here the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, upon his return from one of his military campaigns: "We have returned from the lesser struggle (al-jihad al-asghar) to the greater struggle (al-jihad al-akbar)." So the intended command is "then labour" (fa-insab). As for His saying (﴿fa-idha faraght﴾), it is a preparation and an indication of linking one task to another task in establishing the religion and benefiting the community. This is among the expressions indicating the succession of tasks, similar to the saying of one speaker: "Gifts from so-and-so do not come to me except that another follows them."

The statements of the early exegetes differed in specifying what is meant by that from which one is free, but this is a difference in examples. Thus the omission of the object here is for the purpose of generality, a customary generality covering a category of the tasks indicated by the context, so that it includes every matter to which he devotes his effort that is important, as you know. He is best aware of giving precedence to some tasks over others when many of them cannot be combined as far as possible, just as God permitted the performance of prayer alongside engagement in struggle, in His saying: (﴿And when you are among them and lead them in prayer, let a group of them stand with you﴾ [al-Nisa': 102]) up to His saying: (﴿a decree prescribed in fixed times﴾ [al-Nisa': 103]) in Surat al-Nisa'.

This ruling extends to every feasible task among his particular duties, such as: the night vigil, struggle when the Muslims are strong, and managing the affairs of the community.

The placing of (﴿fa-idha faraght﴾) before (﴿fa-insab﴾) is for the sake of emphasis on tying the work to the time of being free from other things, so that tasks follow one another. This verse is among the comprehensive expressions of the Qur'an, given the abundance of meanings it contains.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 94, verse 8:

﴿And to your Lord direct your longing.﴾

This is conjoined to the consequence of the command to give thanks for blessings: a command to seek the continuation of God's blessings upon him, as God the Exalted said: (﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾ [Ibrahim: 7]).

Al-raghba (desire/longing) is the seeking of the attainment of what is beloved. Its original construction is that the sought object is governed directly, and the thing sought is governed by (fi). It is said: raghiba 'an kadha, meaning he turned his desire away from it by desiring something else. From this is God's saying: (﴿and you desire to marry them﴾ [al-Nisa': 127]), with the omitted preposition before (an) being (ʿan). This is the interpretation of 'A'isha, Mother of the Believers, as already mentioned in Surat al-Nisa'.

As for the verb (fa-arghab) being governed here by (ila), it is because it is made to include the meaning of turning towards and directing oneself, in the manner of a traveller's journey to one who has his need, as God the Exalted said of Abraham: (﴿And he said: Indeed I am going to my Lord﴾ [al-Saffat: 99]).

The fronting of (ila rabbika) before (﴿fa-arghab﴾) serves to express exclusivity, i.e., your desire is toward Him alone and not toward anyone else, since the attribute of prophethood is the greatest of the attributes of creation, and it is not fitting for its bearer to desire other than God the Exalted.

The object of (arghab) is omitted so that it encompasses everything that the Prophet ﷺ desires; and does the Prophet desire anything but perfection of the soul, the spread of the religion, and the victory of the Muslims?

Know that the fa' in His saying (﴿fa-insab﴾ [al-Sharh: 7]) and His saying (﴿fa-arghab﴾) is a connective of the verb; for the fronting of the complement implies the meaning of condition and restriction. When the fronting of the complement conveys exclusivity, the meaning of condition arises from it, and this is frequent in speech. God the Exalted said: (﴿Rather, God alone worship﴾ [al-Zumar: 66]), and He said: (﴿and your Lord, glorify﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 3] ﴿and your garments, purify﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 4] ﴿and uncleanness, forsake﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 5]). And regarding the fronting of the prepositional phrase, God the Exalted said: (﴿and for that let those who compete compete﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 26]). The Prophet ﷺ said to one who asked him to go out for jihad: "Do you have parents? He said: Yes. He said: Then strive with respect to them." Indeed, it may even be treated like a conditional in grammatical analysis, as narrated in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "As you are, so will you be ruled over," with both verbs in the jussive; and this was discussed earlier at God's saying (﴿Let them rejoice in that﴾ [Yunus: 58]) in Surat Yunus.

Al-Tibi reported from the Amali of al-Sayyid, meaning Ibn al-Shajari, that the combination of fa' and waw here is among the most remarkable of their speech; because fa' conjoins or enters the response, and what resembles the response is the incomplete noun, or the verbal relative clause, due to its resemblance to the response, and here it has departed from what it was established for. End of quotation. Nothing remains of wonder after what we have established.

Surat al-Tin

In most books of tafsir and most copies of the Qur'an it is named (Surat wa-al-Tin) with the waw retained, naming it by its first word. Some exegetes named it (Surat al-Tin) without the waw, because the word (al-Tin) occurs in it, as they said (Surat al-Baqara). Al-Tirmidhi and some copies of the Qur'an titled it thus.

It is Meccan according to most scholars. Ibn 'Atiyya said: I know of no disagreement among the exegetes about this, and he did not list it in al-Itqan among the surahs whose classification is disputed. al-Qurtubi mentioned from Qatada that it is Medinan, and this was also attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, but the authentic report from Ibn 'Abbas is that he said: it is Meccan.

It is counted as the twenty-eighth in the order of revelation of the surahs; it was revealed after Surat al-Buruj and before Surat al-Ilaf.

The number of its verses is eight.

* * *

This surah contains: an admonition that God created man upon the upright natural disposition (fitra), so that they may know that Islam is the fitra, as He said in the other verse (﴿So set your face toward the religion, inclining to truth, the fitra of God upon which He created mankind﴾ [al-Rum: 30]); and that whatever opposes its foundations, whether originally or by distortion, is corruption and error, and those who follow what opposes Islam are people of misguidance.

And an allusion to the threat against those who deny Islam.
